deepDives.title: DOE: Over 100 gasoline stations flagged for not reflecting price adjustments
deepDives.summary: More than 100 gasoline stations were found to be non-compliant with imposing price adjustments, the Department of Energy (DOE) said Tuesday.
reasons: reader relevance 3/3: 100+ gas stations flagged for not passing on price cuts

article.text:
More than 100 gasoline stations were found to be non-compliant with imposing price adjustments, the Department of Energy (DOE) said Tuesday.
The DOE- Oil Industry Management Bureau (OIMB) said that it inspected over 200 gasoline stations last week.
"We were able to accumulate around 213 gasoline stations inspected. Unfortunately, 114 of those were found to have not implemented exactly the mandated," said DOE-OIMB director Rino Abad at a press briefing.
The DOE official said that the flagged gasoline stations did not implement the price rollbacks last year. For instance, one gasoline station did not slash gasoline prices by P16.80 per liter, but only by P12 or P10, said Abad.
Gasoline pump prices up; diesel and kerosene down November 3, 2026
Gasoline and kerosene pump prices up Tuesday; diesel down
Oil price rollback likely to continue next week - DOE
After the issuance of show cause orders on the gasoline stations, Abad said that among their reasons for non-compliance was the price set allegedly by the oil firms.
"Most of the cited reason ay yung price na binibigay sa kanilang ng mga head oil companies, yung mother companies, dahil yung mga products na yun ay karamihan doon ay nakuha pa nila last week, which is priced higher than the incoming week," he said.
(Most of the cited reason is the price given to them by the head oil companies, the mother companies, because most of those products were still acquired by them last week, which is priced higher than the incoming week.)
The DOE-OIMB said that they already referred the cases to the legal department for appropriate legal actions.
Under the Downstream Oil Industry Deregulation Act, the government does not directly fix or dictate exact pump prices, although the DOE monitors and publishes recommended price adjustments that companies are expected to reflect.
In March, the DOE directed all oil companies, gasoline stations, and downstream oil industry stakeholders to strictly comply with existing fuel pricing rules and anti-hoarding regulations, "to maintain stability in the domestic petroleum market."
"Gasoline stations are not allowed to implement unscheduled or unauthorized price increases outside established pricing adjustments. Oil companies have likewise been directed to ensure that their company-owned and dealer-operated stations strictly comply with DOE directives, including any duly authorized staggered price adjustments, where applicable," the DOE then said.
Meanwhile, DOE Undersecretary Felix Fuentebella said the public can report erring gas stations via the eGOVPH mobile app.
"We have developed an app sa egov portal, kung saan pwede tayo magsumbong, ire-report natin doon yung ating mga complaints. Pwede rin maglagay ng picture kung ano yung resibo o yung mga nakapaskil para mas maganda yung case build up," he said in the briefing.
(We have developed an app on the egov portal, where we can report, we can report our complaints there. You can also attach a picture of the receipt or what is posted so that the case build-up is better.) — RSJ, GMA News

MANILA, Philippines — Consumption in the Philippines is expected to post a moderate growth of 2.8 percent next year as inflation is likely to remain elevated and weak consumer confidence persists, according to research and analysis firm BMI.
“We maintain a cautiously positive outlook for consumer spending in the Philippines, forecasting real household spending growth of 2.8 percent y-o-y (year-on-year) in 2027 to P14.2 trillion,” the Fitch Solutions unit said in a report yesterday.
If realized, BMI said next year’s spending would be 27.2 percent above the pre-pandemic levels.
The consumption forecast is in line with BMI’s 4.5 percent gross domestic product forecast growth for the country for 2027.
Consumption is the main engine of the Philippine economy.
Household consumption grew by 2.4 percent in the third quarter, slower than the previous quarter’s 2.9 percent growth and four percent expansion in the same quarter last year.
From the first to third quarter, consumption grew by an average of 2.8 percent, also slower than the 4.8 percent growth in the same period in 2025.
BMI said that household spending next year would be supported by the availability of more jobs in the market and the faster growth in wages compared to living costs.
However, it flagged high inflation as a risk to the outlook, warning that the conflict between the United States (US) and Iran could place upward pressure on energy prices, while a weak peso, severe El Niño conditions and widening second-round price effects could keep inflation elevated.
BMI said it expects inflation to ease to 5.4 percent next year from its 5.9 percent forecast for this year.
Overall inflation accelerated to 7.8 percent in October, the highest level in almost four years, driven by higher energy and transport costs.
From January to October, inflation averaged 5.6 percent, above the government’s two to four percent target band for the year.
Apart from elevated inflation, BMI said high household debt and debt-servicing costs may limit consumption growth next year.
BMI said consumer confidence also remains sluggish, although not at the level of weakness seen during the COVID-19 pandemic years when the confidence index was at -54.5 percent.
While the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ survey showed that consumer confidence improved to -29.8 in the third quarter from the six-year low reading of -42 percent in the second quarter, BMI said it was still the worst performance since the first quarter of 2021.
“Consumer confidence remains weak as households braced for higher fuel and food costs stemming from the Middle East conflict, while also contending with weaker economic conditions, rising unemployment and a depreciating Philippine peso,” BMI said.
Governance issues and the perception that the government is not doing enough to curb price pressures also continue to weigh on consumer confidence.
BMI said remittances, which remain an important source of income for many households, also face several downside risks next year, particularly from potential economic and financial stress in major source markets.
The US remains the Philippines’ top source of remittances, accounting for around 40 percent of the total, followed by Singapore (7.3 percent), Saudi Arabia (6.6 percent) and Japan and the United Kingdom (five percent each).
“This leaves household remittance income exposed to weaker economic conditions in these markets, particularly the US,” BMI said.
However, it said continued peso weakness heading into 2027 would increase the local currency value of remittances.
BMI expects the peso to depreciate against the dollar next year to P62.7 from an average of P61.2 this year.
Amid headwinds from a highly uncertain and increasingly volatile macroeconomic environment next year, BMI said consumers are likely to be cautious in terms of spending and prioritize essential services.
“Thus, consumers will seek out value-oriented options and become increasingly selective in their purchasing decisions throughout 2027,” BMI said.

MANILA, Philippines — The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is proposing tougher capital and licensing rules for remittance companies and money changers, potentially raising compliance costs for smaller operators as it strengthens oversight of nonbank financial services.
Under draft amendments to its regulations, remittance and transfer companies (RTCs), which facilitate domestic and overseas money transfers, will have a base capital requirement of P50 million. Money changers and foreign exchange dealers will have a P10-million requirement.
Existing rules set those capital benchmarks for large-scale operators, defined as remittance firms processing at least P75 million in average monthly transactions and currency dealers handling at least P50 million. Smaller operators are classified as having capital below those levels.
The proposal removes the separate small- and large-scale capital classifications, although the draft retains transaction thresholds for determining which firms face enhanced assessments.
RTCs exceeding P75 million in average monthly network transactions and money changers exceeding P50 million will also need an operational buffer equivalent to at least six months of projected expenses, on top of minimum capital.
The BSP said the changes address risks arising from the industry’s “increasing scale, evolving risk exposures and greater operational complexity.”
The draft will also require all money service businesses (MSBs) – a category that includes remittance providers, currency dealers, nonbank electronic money issuers and virtual asset service providers – to be organized as regular stock corporations incorporated in the Philippines.
Sole proprietorships, partnerships, cooperatives, non-stock corporations and one-person corporations will no longer qualify, requiring affected existing firms to restructure.
Licensing fees for small remittance companies will rise fivefold to P100,000 from P20,000, while those for small money changers will increase to P50,000 from P20,000. The fee for large money changers, however, will fall to P50,000 from P100,000.
Annual supervisory fees will remain unchanged at P100,000 and P20,000, respectively.
Applicants will face closer scrutiny of their financial capacity, risk management and shareholders, including ultimate beneficial owners.
Existing operators will have two years from the rules’ effectivity to meet the new requirements and obtain fresh authority. Those failing to comply will have to cease regulated operations.
The BSP can also restrict expansion or new products for firms with capital shortfalls and require plans to restore adequate capital.

article.text:
The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is proposing stricter licensing and capital rules for remittance firms, money changers, e-money issuers, and crypto service providers, including a mandatory QR code system to help customers verify whether operators are authorized to do business.Under a proposed circular, the BSP is looking to have money service businesses (MSBs) obtain a new Certificate of Authority within two years, or stop operating.
Remittance firms would need at least P50 million in base capital, and money changers P10 million.Applicants would pay a P1,000 application fee, then a non-refundable licensing fee once approved: P100,000 for e-money issuers, crypto service providers, and remittance firms, and P50,000 for money changers.Annual supervisory fees would range from P20,000 to P300,000, depending on the license type and transaction volume.Should the applications be approved, licensed firms would also have to display a QR code in their offices and mobile apps so that customers can check their license against the BSP registry.Applicants would also face closer scrutiny of ownership, as the proposed circular would give the BSP the authority to assess the fitness and propriety of directors, senior managers, and substantial shareholders, including ultimate beneficial owners, and examine the source of their funds.Bigger firms would also be required to keep a cushion equivalent to at least six months of operating expenses on top of minimum capital.The proposal would also limit who can operate, as money service businesses could only act as regular stock corporations, ruling out sole proprietorships, cooperatives, and one-person corporations.Existing firms organized in the same way would have to set up or convert into a compliant entity and apply for a new license in its name, with BSP approval required to transfer operations, assets, and customer obligations.“(T)he Bangko Sentral aims to implement enabling regulations that supports the growth of the MSB sector and promote a broad access to high-quality financial services while safeguarding the interests of the general public and maintaining the integrity of the financial system,” the draft circular read.The draft circular will be available for public comment until Friday, November 20, 2026. —VAL, GMA News

quickHits.summary: The Philippine peso nearly touched the P64-to-$1 level on Tuesday as the greenback"s strength continues to weigh on the local unit.

article.text:
The Philippine peso nearly touched the P64-to-$1 level on Tuesday as the greenback’s strength continues to weigh on the local unit.
The local currency hit a low of P63.99:$1 and a high of P63.73:$1 during intraday trading.
The US dollar was supported by hawkish Federal Reserve expectations, elevated US Treasury yields, and geopolitical uncertainties, according to Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. chief economist Michael Ricafort
The peso opened at P63.9:$1, from its previous close of P63.94:$1.
Peso claws back P62-to-$1 level on lower oil prices
It closed at P63.67:$. The previous close on Monday was P63.94:$1.
Meanwhile, the recent decline in global crude oil prices amid signals of increased global supplies led the peso to close stronger, said Ricafort.
Ricafort said possible rate hikes by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas could “somewhat help stabilize the peso exchange rate, importation costs, and, in turn, also better manage inflation and inflation expectations.” —AOL/NB, GMA News

MANILA, Philippines — The country has imported more than four million metric tons (MT) of rice as of October, with volumes nearing record-high levels as the country builds up stock due to production constraints caused by El Niño.
Data from the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI) showed that rice import arrivals surged to 4.49 million MT as of Oct.29, approaching the record 4.48 million MT imported during the 2024 El Niño year.
The import volume of grain that entered the country from January to October has already surpassed the 3.39 million MT total rice imports recorded last year.
Among the top sources of rice during the 10-month period was Vietnam, accounting for more than half of all imports, at 2.79 million MT.
It was followed by Thailand at 666,201 MT and Myanmar at 505,740 MT.

To strengthen preparedness against supply disruptions
THE Department of Energy said Tuesday that the Philippines and Japan had signed a memorandum of cooperation (MOC) “to advance the development of the country’s strategic petroleum reserves, strengthening national preparedness against global oil supply disruptions and helping safeguard fuel availability for Filipino consumers, businesses, and industries.”
In a statement, the agency said the agreement provided a framework for establishing systems to build, manage, and release strategic petroleum reserves, taking into account the Philippines’ fuel supply and demand requirements, market conditions, and the need for effective emergency response mechanisms.
Under the cooperation, both countries will explore the development of oil storage infrastructure, including potential participation of Japanese companies in Philippine National Oil Company (PNOC)-led commercial stockpiling projects.
The agreement also covers the development of strategic petroleum reserve facilities based on ongoing feasibility studies and the identification of possible financing arrangements.
Moreover, technical cooperation will draw on ongoing initiatives involving the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (Jogmec), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and the Economic Research Institute for Asean and East Asia (ERIA).
